passages.t: ‘Did God reject His people?’ The remnant
passages.happening:
Paul asks the question chapter 10 has raised. “I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin” (verse 1). “God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew” (verse 2).

He reminds them of Elijah, who complained to God that Israel had killed the prophets, and said, “I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well” (verse 3). God answered, “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal” (verse 4). “In the same way, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace” (verse 5). And if it is by grace, it is not by works, or grace would no longer be grace (verse 6).

What Israel sought, it did not obtain, but the chosen did. “The others were hardened” (verse 7), as Scripture says: God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that could not see and ears that could not hear (verse 8). David says, “May their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution to them” (verse 9), and may their eyes be darkened (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Paul's first answer is himself. He is a Jew who believes in Jesus. So God has not thrown Israel away. The first believers in Jerusalem were all Jews, and Jewish believers sat in the house churches of Rome as Paul's letter was read.

‘Foreknew’ is the word Paul used in 8:29 for God's loving choice of his people. Here he uses it of Israel. God knew this people and set his love on them long ago. He did not do that by mistake, and he does not undo it.

Elijah felt utterly alone. He thought he was the last faithful man in Israel. He was wrong. God had seven thousand. A ‘remnant’ means what is left, a faithful part that God keeps. In Paul's day, too, many Jews had believed: in Jerusalem, in Antioch, in Rome itself.

‘Hardened’ means made dull or unresponsive. Paul does not say this with pleasure. He has just said he would give up his own place in Christ for them (9:3). And he will say at once that the hardening is not the end.
passages.ot:
Verses 3 and 4 come from 1 Kings 19. Elijah had fled into the wilderness after Queen Jezebel threatened his life. He said, “I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well” (1 Kings 19:10). God's answer was, “Nevertheless, I have reserved seven thousand in Israel” (1 Kings 19:18).

Verse 8 joins Moses and Isaiah. Moses told Israel, “Yet to this day the LORD has not given you a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear” (Deuteronomy 29:4). Isaiah said, “For the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep” (Isaiah 29:10). Paul quotes them in the Greek wording, which has ‘stupor’.

Verses 9 and 10 quote Psalm 69, a psalm of a righteous sufferer surrounded by enemies: “May their table become a snare” (Psalm 69:22), and “May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent forever” (Psalm 69:23). The New Testament reads Psalm 69 often in the light of Jesus' sufferings. The site's note on Psalm 69 explains how these hard lines are used here.
passages.hard:
What does Paul mean by quoting Psalm 69's curse here? The site's note on Psalm 69 says it plainly. Paul quotes verses 22 and 23 in Romans 11:9-10, writing about those among his own people who did not believe in Jesus. He writes with grief, not scorn: “I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (Romans 9:2). And he says at once that this is not the end: “did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:11). The hardening is only “in part” and for a time (Romans 11:25). These verses give no one any reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people, and Paul himself warns his readers against pride (Romans 11:25).

Notice two small words that come later in the chapter: ‘in part’ and ‘until’. “A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in” (verse 25). Paul does not say all Israel is hardened, and he does not say it is forever.

Readers differ on how God's hardening relates to human refusal, as they do in 9:18. Some see God's free decision first; others see God confirming a refusal already made. These notes do not choose.
passages.asks: Elijah thought he was alone, and he was wrong. Ask where you have decided that you are the only faithful one left, in a family, a church or a town. Ask God to show you the others he has kept.

passages.t: A stumble, not a fall: ‘to make Israel jealous’
passages.happening:
“I ask then, did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Certainly not! However, because of their trespass, salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous” (verse 11).

If their stumbling has brought riches to the world, “how much greater riches will their fullness bring!” (verse 12).

Paul turns to the Gentile believers. “I am speaking to you Gentiles” (verse 13). He works hard as apostle to the Gentiles in the hope of moving his own people to jealousy and saving some of them (verse 14). “For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?” (verse 15).

“If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch; if the root is holy, so are the branches” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
A stumble is not a fall. A runner who trips can get up and finish. Paul's question in verse 11 expects the answer no, and he gives it.

Here is Paul's surprising picture of history. Israel's ‘no’ to Jesus opened the door for the message to go to the nations. And the nations' coming in is meant, in turn, to make Israel jealous, wanting what it sees, and so to bring Israel back. Paul calls that return their ‘fullness’ and ‘acceptance’, and he says it will be like ‘life from the dead’.

Notice who Paul is speaking to: ‘you Gentiles’. These words are for the non-Jewish believers in Rome. Paul is not telling them they have taken Israel's place. He is telling them their own mission serves Israel's future.

Verse 16 uses two pictures. When Israel baked, the first piece of dough was offered to God, and that made the whole batch holy. And a holy root makes holy branches. Many readers take the first part and the root to be the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, with whom God made his promises.
passages.ot:
The ‘first part of the dough’ comes from the law of Moses: “From the first of your dough, you are to lift up a cake as a contribution” (Numbers 15:20). The offering of the first part showed that the whole belonged to God.

‘Jealous’ picks up the Song of Moses, which Paul quoted in 10:19: “So I will make them jealous by those who are not a people” (Deuteronomy 32:21). In the song, God uses outsiders to wake his people.

The prophets also saw the nations coming to Israel's God. Isaiah's servant was called to be “a light to the nations” (Isaiah 42:6). Paul sees that happening, and he believes it will lead back to Israel, not away from it.
passages.hard:
Has the church replaced Israel? Christians have answered this in different ways. Here are the main views, each in its holders' terms. These notes do not choose.

Replacement theology, also called supersessionism, holds that the church has taken Israel's place as God's people. Much of the church held it for centuries, often in harsh forms, and many churches now reject it. Others, especially in Reformed churches, hold a milder form they call fulfilment: God's promises to Israel are fulfilled in Christ, and Israel and the church are one people of God in him.

Covenant theology stresses one people of God across both Testaments, one olive tree with Jewish and Gentile branches. Many who hold it also expect a future turning of Jewish people to Christ.

Dispensational readings hold that God keeps a distinct future for ethnic Israel, the Jewish people, beside the church, with promises still to be fulfilled.

Two-covenant readings, held by some and not by most churches, say Jews are in covenant with God through Moses and need not come to faith in Christ. Most readers answer that verse 23 and verse 27 speak of unbelief ended and sins taken away.

In 1965 the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council cited verses 28 and 29 and said that God holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their fathers.

On every view, contempt for Jews has no ground in these chapters. Paul forbids Gentile boasting (verses 18-21). For centuries some Christians used the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. Nothing here is a claim about any modern state.
passages.asks: Paul hoped his work among Gentiles would move his own people to want what they saw. Ask what your life shows to people who do not share your faith: something to want, or something to avoid.

passages.happening:
Paul paints a picture. Some branches of an olive tree have been broken off. You Gentiles, a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others to share in the rich root (verse 17).

Paul warns, “do not boast over those branches. If you do, remember this: You do not support the root, but the root supports you” (verse 18).

You may say branches were broken off so that you could be grafted in. “That is correct: They were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but be afraid” (verse 20). If God did not spare the natural branches, he will not spare you either (verse 21).

“Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God” (verse 22): severity to those who fell, kindness to you, if you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off. And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to do it (verse 23). If you were grafted, contrary to nature, from a wild tree into a cultivated one, how much more readily will the natural branches be grafted back into their own olive tree (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Olive trees grew everywhere around the Mediterranean. Olive oil was food, lamp oil, medicine and soap. Everyone knew the trees, gnarled and old, living for centuries.

‘Grafting’ means cutting a branch from one tree and setting it into another so that it grows there. Gardeners usually set a good, cultivated shoot onto a wild root. Paul pictures the reverse: wild branches set into a good tree. He says himself that it is ‘contrary to nature’. Whether he had any farming practice in mind is debated. His point is not gardening. It is grace. The Gentiles had no natural claim to this tree at all.

The tree is not the church replacing Israel. It is Israel's own tree, rooted in God's promises to the patriarchs. Gentile believers have been brought into it. The natural branches still belong to it: Paul calls it ‘their own olive tree’.

The warning was pointed. If the house churches in Rome had become mostly Gentile, some Gentile believers may have begun to look down on Jews, believing or not. Paul tells them: you are held up by a Jewish root. You stand by faith, not by birth. Fear God, and do not boast.
passages.ot:
Israel's prophets called Israel an olive tree. Jeremiah says, “The LORD once called you a flourishing olive tree, beautiful with well-formed fruit” (Jeremiah 11:16), and then warns that its branches will be burned for the people's sins. Hosea promises restoration: “his splendor will be like the olive tree” (Hosea 14:6).

So Paul's picture is drawn from Scripture. The tree is God's people Israel. Branches can be broken off, as Jeremiah warned, and restored, as Hosea promised. What is new in Paul is the wild branches: Gentiles brought into Israel's tree by faith.
passages.hard:
‘Otherwise you also will be cut off’ (verse 22). Can a believer fall away? Readers who hold different views take these verses differently. These notes do not choose.

Those who hold that a person truly saved cannot finally be lost, much of the Reformed and Baptist world, often read Paul as speaking of Gentiles as a group, not of each person. Or they read the warning as one of the means God uses to keep his people: true believers heed it and continue. They hold that those who fall away show that they never truly belonged.

Those who hold that a person can turn away and forfeit salvation, much of the Wesleyan, Arminian and Catholic world, read the warning at face value. A branch that was truly part of the tree can be cut off through unbelief. They note that it cuts both ways: a broken branch can also be grafted back in (verse 23).

Both agree on Paul's main point: no one stands by birth or by merit, only by faith, and no believer may look down on anyone. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Can you lose your salvation?’, sets out both cases.

And both agree on the warning Paul gives Gentile believers. Arrogance toward the Jewish people is forbidden by this passage. “You do not support the root, but the root supports you” (verse 18).
passages.asks: ‘The root supports you.’ Ask what you owe to the Jewish people: the Scriptures, the promises, the Messiah himself. Then ask how that should shape the way you speak about Jewish people, and to them.

passages.t: ‘All Israel will be saved’: the gifts and the call
passages.happening:
Paul tells the Gentile believers a mystery, so that they will not be conceited. “A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in” (verse 25).

“And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: ‘The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob’” (verse 26). “And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins” (verse 27).

As far as the gospel goes, they are enemies for your sake, “but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs” (verse 28). “For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
In Paul's letters, a ‘mystery’ is not a puzzle. It is something God had kept hidden and has now made known. Paul gives this one for a reason: ‘so that you will not be conceited’. It is a word against Gentile pride.

The mystery has three parts. A hardening has come on part of Israel. It lasts until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved.

‘Enemies’ in verse 28 does not mean Paul's enemies, or the church's. It means that, as things stand, many in Israel are opposed to the gospel, and that this has opened the way for Gentiles: ‘for your sake’. In the same breath Paul says they are ‘loved’, because of God's promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

‘Irrevocable’ means cannot be taken back. God does not change his mind about his gifts to Israel or his call of Israel. For the Gentile believers in Rome that was a comfort too. If God could cancel his promises to Israel, he could cancel his promises to them.
passages.ot:
Verses 26 and 27 join several prophecies. The first is Isaiah 59. In the Berean Standard Bible's Hebrew-based wording it reads, “The Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression” (Isaiah 59:20). Paul follows the Greek translation, which differs: the Deliverer comes ‘from Zion’ and removes godlessness ‘from Jacob’. In both, God himself comes to save his people. Isaiah goes on, “As for Me, this is My covenant with them” (Isaiah 59:21).

The words ‘when I take away their sins’ recall Isaiah 27: “Therefore Jacob’s guilt will be atoned for” (Isaiah 27:9). Many readers also hear the new covenant of Jeremiah, where God promises, “For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (Jeremiah 31:34).

‘Loved on account of the patriarchs’ goes back to Moses: God set his love on Israel “because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers” (Deuteronomy 7:8).
passages.hard:
What does ‘all Israel will be saved’ mean? Christians read verse 26 in more than one way. These notes do not choose, or say how the promise will be fulfilled.

Many think it promises a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end, often linked with his return. They note that ‘Israel’ in verse 25 means the Jewish people, and so likely does in verse 26, and that the natural branches will be grafted back in (verse 23).

Others take ‘all Israel’ to mean the whole people of God, Jews and Gentiles together. They point to Paul's words that “not all who are descended from Israel are Israel” (Romans 9:6), and to ‘the Israel of God’ in Galatians 6:16.

Others take it to mean the full number of Jewish believers through all of history, the remnant gathered over time, so that verse 26 describes how God saves Israel through the whole age.

Readers also differ on ‘And so’: it may mean ‘in this way’ or ‘after this’.

On any reading, Paul's own words stand: “God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew” (Romans 11:2), and “God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (verse 29). This passage is about God's faithfulness. It makes no claim about any modern state, border or conflict, and these notes make none. The book page's hard passage on 11:26 says the same.
passages.asks: If God keeps his promises to Israel through centuries of stumbling, he will keep them to you. Ask what promise of God you have stopped expecting. Read verse 29 again, and hold it out to him.

passages.t: Mercy on everyone, and ‘O, the depth’
passages.happening:
Paul gathers the whole argument in two sentences. Gentiles once disobeyed God and have now received mercy through Israel's disobedience (verse 30). So Israel too has disobeyed, so that they too may now receive mercy through the mercy shown to the Gentiles (verse 31). “For God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone” (verse 32).

Then the argument breaks into praise. “O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!” (verse 33).

“Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?” (verse 34). “Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?” (verse 35). “For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever! Amen” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
‘Consigned’ means shut up, as in a prison. Paul says Jews and Gentiles alike have been shut up together under disobedience. No one stands on higher ground. And the door out is the same for both: mercy.

After three chapters of hard argument, Paul does not end with a chart of the future or a tidy system. He ends on his knees. The questions of chapters 9 to 11 have not all been answered. Paul's answer is worship. God's ways are deeper than anyone can trace, and he owes no one anything.

The three questions in verses 34 and 35 each expect the answer ‘no one’. No one has known God's mind from the inside. No one has advised him. No one has given him something so that he owes them in return.

‘From Him and through Him and to Him’. Everything comes from God, holds together through God, and goes back to God. The listeners in Rome, Jew and Gentile, would have said the ‘Amen’ together.
passages.ot:
Verse 34 quotes Isaiah: “Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or informed Him as His counselor?” (Isaiah 40:13). In Isaiah 40 these words come just after the promise of comfort to Israel in exile. God's greatness is the reason his people can trust him.

Verse 35 seems to echo God's words in Job: “Who has given to Me that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is Mine” (Job 41:11). Job had wanted God to answer him. God answered with questions that showed his greatness. Paul uses the line in the same spirit.

The whole doxology, a short hymn of praise, sounds like the praises of the Psalms. The Psalms often end a hard prayer with blessing God.
passages.hard:
Does ‘mercy on everyone’ in verse 32 mean that every person will in the end be saved? Christians read it in different ways, as they read ‘all’ in 5:18.

Christian universalists take ‘everyone’ in its full sense: God will in the end have mercy on every person. Some Christians, from early times to today, have held or hoped for this; most churches have not taught it.

Many other readers note that in this chapter Paul is speaking of two groups, Jews and Gentiles. On this reading, ‘everyone’ means both groups, not every single person: God's way of dealing with Jew and Gentile alike is mercy. Reformed readers often add that the mercy comes to those God calls; Arminian and Wesleyan readers that it is offered to all and received by faith.

These notes set out the readings and do not choose. The note on Romans 5:15-21 sets out the same readings, and the site's Honest Answer, ‘Is hell forever, or does it end?’, takes up the related questions.

What all agree on is where Paul ends: not with a system, but with worship.
passages.asks: Paul's hardest thinking ended in praise. Take a question about God that you cannot settle. Without dropping it, read verses 33 to 36 aloud, and let them be your prayer for today.
